title: The hymn that starts with questions
hookLine: rewind everything until there's nothing left to rewind. The Rig Veda's hymn of creation starts there, and starts with questions
carry: the big questions are kept inside scripture
tomorrow: before night and day, was anything there at all?
last: THE GAMBLER'S HYMN: FARM YOUR FIELD.

cards: Run the day backward, like a video on rewind. Dinner un-cooks. The drive home un-drives.
Morning coffee pours itself back into the pot. Keep going. The house comes apart into lumber, the lumber into trees, the trees into seeds.
Past the first people, the first mountains, the first stars. At some point the rewind has nothing left to rewind. What's there?
Or is there even a there? One Rig Veda hymn stops at that last frame and stares at it. You glimpsed it on day one thousand fifty-seven.

teach.b: The hymn takes its name from its first words, na asat: not non-being.
In paraphrase it opens: then there was not non-being, and there was not being. There was no air, and no sky beyond it. It doesn't say, in the beginning there was nothing.
It says even nothing wasn't there yet. The usual pair of opposites, is and isn't, hasn't started. And then, instead of an answer, the poet asks questions.

teach.h: WHAT COVERED IT? WHERE? IN WHOSE CARE?
teach.b: What covered it? Where? In whose keeping?
Was there water, deep beyond measure? That's the whole first verse: a hymn about creation that begins by refusing to describe it, and asks instead. Some readers hear wonder in that.
Some hear a careful thinker, unwilling to claim more than anyone could know. Some Hindu teachers hear a picture of Brahman before names and forms. The hymn doesn't say which.
It simply puts the questions into the sacred collection, to be chanted. They weren't left at the edge of scripture as doubts. They were kept inside it.
Hinduism has no single creation story you must sign on to: the Rig Veda alone holds several, and the Puranas tell more.
And honest asking is treated as holy. Many Upanishads are built as conversations, a student asking, a teacher answering. In this tradition the question isn't the enemy of faith.

how: The Nasadiya Sukta is chanted as part of the Rig Veda's recited text and is also studied and discussed by Hindu teachers as a reflection on what came before creation.

o: the Rig Veda's hymn of creation, full of questions
a hymn praising the god who built the world
a chant to keep away the dark at night

games.q: the hymn's first verse — tap the pairs.
p: not non-being: the hymn's first words

s: the hymn's name comes from its first words
Nasadiya, from na asat: not non-being.
the first verse says there was empty nothing
it says there was not non-being, and not being either: even nothing wasn't there yet.
the first verse ends with an answer
it ends with questions: what covered it, where, in whose keeping, was there water?

games.q: you're the poet. you've just said there was no being, no non-being, no air, no sky. what do you write next?
o: the name of the god who made it all.
the order in which things were made.
games.why: the first verse turns to questions: what covered it? where? in whose keeping? was there water, deep beyond measure?

practice: Let one large question come, the hymn's own if you like: what was here before anything? When an answer offers itself, set it down gently and ask again, keeping the question the way the hymn keeps its questions, open and cared for.
If you pray, you can hold the question in that presence.

wordCard.voice: The Nasadiya Sukta. The Rig Veda's hymn of creation, named from its first words, not non-being, which opens with questions instead of answers.

orig.note: Sanskrit: from na asat, not non-being, the hymn's opening words. Sukta means hymn.

carryVoice: Here's your line: the big questions are kept inside scripture. The creation hymn answers with questions. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.129.1 (then there was not non-being, nor being; no air, nor sky beyond; what covered it, where, in whose keeping; was there water, unfathomably deep?)
Rig Veda 10.90 (Purusha Sukta) and 10.121 (the Hiranyagarbha hymn): other Rig Veda accounts of the beginning, referred to only as a group
